review_theme: Dye streak as an indication of orderly motion
teacher_note: A narrow persistent streak is evidence consistent with a smooth streamline/laminar demonstration, although diffusion, dye injection and local turbulence affect appearance; it is not conclusive evidence for all regions of the flow.

review_theme: Irregular swirling and mixing
teacher_note: Rapid, irregular dye spreading and swirls favor the turbulent-flow option among the original four. Contrast turbulent disorder with steady laminar paths, without implying every vortex is turbulent.

review_theme: Local eddies do not independently prove turbulence
teacher_note: Rotating regions downstream of a rock are eddies and likely disturbed wake flow, so D is best among four alternatives. In general a vortex may exist in laminar flow; eddies alone do not mathematically certify turbulent flow, which has additional irregular/fluctuating features.

review_theme: Aerodynamic streamlining and official B-35 scope
teacher_note: A smoother vehicle front can reduce wake disturbance and aerodynamic form drag under comparable conditions, supporting original D. A wind-tunnel design question is not a direct test of B-35's steady/incompressible/non-viscous terms; B-42 is a possible topic alignment only pending exact per-item teacher review.

review_theme: Fish shape and hydrodynamic resistance
teacher_note: A smoother streamlined fish shape can reduce resistance under comparable fluid and speed conditions, so A is best. This real-body drag application is not automatically a direct official B-35 ideal-fluid definition item; candidate B-42 requires approval and cannot be assumed.

review_theme: Abrupt valve changes and observed swirls
teacher_note: An abrupt change can disturb otherwise ordered motion, and the stem specifically says swirling is observed. Such changes do not necessarily cause turbulence for every Reynolds number; the prepared 'NBF description' phrase has not been checked against printed NBF pp.95–96.

review_theme: Incompressible and inviscid independent assumptions
teacher_note: Constant density and neglected internal viscous shear match the simplified ideal-fluid model. Density and viscosity remain distinct; an inviscid model does not require absence of matter.

review_theme: Streamline crossing and local velocity
teacher_note: A velocity field with a well-defined nonzero local velocity cannot have crossing streamlines with incompatible directions. At a stagnation point a direction may be undefined, but this does not rescue the conflicting arrows in the stated animation.

review_theme: Density variation invalidates incompressible approximation
teacher_note: Strong compression substantially changing a material sample's density violates the intended constant-density approximation. Fluidity and SI units are unrelated to the idealization.

review_theme: Real honey viscosity versus inviscid model
teacher_note: Honey's considerable shear resistance makes a zero-viscosity approximation inappropriate for its actual slow flow. B-41 is a possible accompanying real-fluid SLO, but item-level classification is still pending.

review_theme: Local differences in flow character
teacher_note: An obstacle can create a disturbed region near an otherwise smooth channel. A river need not have the same flow regime everywhere, and a local eddy does not prove zero viscosity.

review_theme: Streamlined attachment as engineering response
teacher_note: A more streamlined attachment is a sensible change to test for wake reduction; actual drag benefit depends on geometry, orientation and Reynolds number. This design response does not directly define an ideal-fluid property in B-35; individual B-42 alternative mapping needs teacher approval.

review_theme: Steady flow is local time invariance
teacher_note: A fixed location P has the same local velocity for each passing particle under a steady field. This does not require one identical velocity at every position in the entire flow.

review_theme: Laminar does not mean spatially uniform velocity
teacher_note: Different smooth layers can have distinct speeds without disrupting laminar order. A pressure-driven no-slip pipe usually has faster flow away from walls, but not every laminar arrangement shares one prescribed profile.

review_theme: Critical transition depends on Reynolds and setup
teacher_note: Increased pump speed may lead to turbulence in the depicted setup, so C is best. There is no universal sharp critical speed that governs all fluids and conduits; transition depends on geometry, disturbances, fluid properties and Reynolds number.

review_theme: Inviscid does not mean density-free
teacher_note: Viscosity and mass density have different units and meanings. Neglecting shear resistance does not eliminate mass per volume, so original A is correct.

review_theme: Swimmer drag reduction and exact summative coverage
teacher_note: A streamlined profile can reduce water resistance, supporting B under otherwise comparable motion. The athlete design example does not directly assess B-35's listed ideal-fluid terms, and any B-42 candidate linkage needs individual SLO confirmation.

review_theme: 18 L over 6 s measures flow rate rather than speed
teacher_note: 18/6 = 3 L/s is average volumetric flow rate, not a particle speed 3 m/s; the original B is correct. The Q=V/t question is useful practice but does not directly test B-35's named ideal-fluid terms or B-36's two-section equation of continuity; exam certification remains pending.

review_theme: Local steady velocity for successive particles
teacher_note: Steady flow means same velocity at the same fixed point over time, not a globally constant velocity field or zero speed. Original D matches this local criterion.

teacher_note: The prepared teacher master answer key says Figure6.6(a) depicts streamline flow and (b) turbulence, so B matches prepared-source letter.
